title: Chapter LV

teacherSummary.text: Bingley proposes to Jane, who is overjoyed. Mr. Bennet jokes that they are so easy-going every servant will cheat them. The family celebrates.

vocabulary.definition: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner
vocabulary.context: Kitty simpered and smiled, and hoped her turn was coming soon.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “simper”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement
vocabulary.context: This naturally introduced a panegyric from Jane on his diffidence, and the little value he put on his own good qualities.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “panegyric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of meditating or contriving beforehand
vocabulary.context: Jane instantly gave a look at Elizabeth, which spoke her distress at such premeditation, and her entreaty that she would not give into it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “premeditation”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Your tempers are by no means unlike.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “temper”: temp (Latin tempus, "time") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Her younger sisters soon began to make interest with her for objects of happiness which she might in future be able to dispense.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dispense”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + pens (Latin pendere, "to weigh, pay"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Deviating or departing from the center, or from the line of a circle
vocabulary.context: There was nothing of presumption or folly in Bingley that could provoke his ridicule, or disgust him into silence; and he was more communicative, and less eccentric than the other had ever seen him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “eccentric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Openly declared, avowed, acknowledged, or claimed
vocabulary.context: Bingley was everything that was charming, except the professed lover of her daughter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “professed”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Jane could have no reserves from Elizabeth, where confidence would give pleasure; and instantly embracing her, acknowledged, with the liveliest emotion, that she was the happiest creature in the world.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “embrace”: em- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Not a word, however, passed his lips in allusion to it, till their visitor took his leave for the night; but as soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “allusion”: -sion (Latin -sio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Possessed of genius, or the faculty of invention
vocabulary.context: But on returning to the drawing-room, when her letter was finished, she saw, to her infinite surprise, there was reason to fear that her mother had been too ingenious for her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ingenious”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + gen (Latin/Greek genus, "birth, kind") + -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

significance: Jane's happiness rewards her patience and goodness.
discussionQuestions: Do Jane and Bingley deserve each other? Why?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

items.prompt: In the line “Kitty simpered and smiled, and hoped her turn was coming soon.”, what does “simpered” most nearly mean?
options: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner
The act of meditating or contriving beforehand
An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement

items.prompt: In the line “This naturally introduced a panegyric from Jane on his diffidence, and the little value he put on his own good qualities.”, what does “panegyric” most nearly mean?
options: The act of meditating or contriving beforehand
An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement
To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner

answerKey.answer: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner
An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LV,” how does Austen show happiness for Jane? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LV, how does Austen develop the idea of happiness for Jane? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LV develops the idea of happiness for Jane. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of happiness for Jane. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LV suggests about happiness for Jane. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter LV to complicate the reader's understanding of happiness for Jane. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of happiness for Jane responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of happiness for Jane follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LV and its treatment of happiness for Jane. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LV as evidence for a larger claim about happiness for Jane in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of happiness for Jane. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.passage: She then sat still five minutes longer; but unable to waste such a precious occasion, she suddenly got up, and saying to Kitty, “Come here, my love, I want to speak to you,” took her out of the room. Jane instantly gave a look at Elizabeth, which spoke her distress at such premeditation, and her entreaty that she would not give into it.

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Do Jane and Bingley deserve each other? Why? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are simpered, panegyric, premeditation, tempers, dispense. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Kitty simpered and smiled, and hoped her turn was coming soon.” Webster's says: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner. Now the word history: “simper”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “panegyric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “premeditation”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Engagements needed the father's consent. Why does this chapter matter? Jane's happiness rewards her patience and goodness. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to happiness for Jane.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: She then sat still five minutes longer; but unable to waste such a precious occasion, she suddenly got up, and saying to Kitty, “Come here, my love, I want to speak to you,” took her out of the room. Jane instantly gave a look at Elizabeth, which spoke her distress at such premeditation, and her entreaty that she would not give into it.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Plot, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LV,” how does Austen show happiness for Jane? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about happiness for Jane, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes happiness for Jane. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
